summary: The Rabbanan explain their ketoret-first ruling via a parallel from the afternoon service: 'at the time of lighting you shall burn the incense,' meaning incense accompanies the lamp service - not after it. Abba Shaul rejects this analogy ('oto' limits the afternoon rule). Rav Pappa and Abaye offer competing resolutions to the three-clause mishna contradiction; they disagree on whether a mishna can mix tannaitic positions mid-text. The Gemara then examines the basis for Rabbi Shimon ish HaMitzpah's unique tamid blood-sprinkling method - the verse commands that the tamid be performed like both an olah and a chatat simultaneously. A series of proposals for how to execute this dual requirement are raised and refuted, each failing on the principle that we have no precedent for blood that both atones and re-atones.

display.title: One word, 'oto', decides whether the afternoon proof reaches the morning
display.oneLine: The Rabbanan extend the afternoon lamp-incense verse to prove ketoret comes first in the morning too; Abba Shaul reads 'oto' as blocking that extension.
display.whats: The Rabbanan defend their position that ketoret (incense) is burned before the lamps by drawing a parallel from the afternoon tamid: 'at the time of lighting you shall burn incense' means the incense accompanies the lamp service. Abba Shaul objects that 'oto' (that specific lamp) limits this rule to the afternoon only, not the morning.
display.hint: The word 'oto' in the verse - 'and when Aaron lights it' - is doing a lot of work. The Rabbanan read it as an analogy; Abba Shaul reads it as a restriction.

learning.learnerQuestion: The Rabbanan say ketoret comes before the lamps, citing a verse about the afternoon service. Why does that afternoon verse prove anything about the morning order?
learning.coreTension: The Rabbanan treat the afternoon lamp-incense verse as a general principle that also governs the morning, while Abba Shaul reads the same verse's word 'oto' as confining it strictly to the afternoon case.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara first reads 'at the time of lighting' as meaning incense accompanies the lamps rather than following them, supporting the Rabbanan's analogy; Abba Shaul then isolates the word 'oto' (that one lamp) to argue the verse cannot be generalized beyond its stated afternoon context.
learning.learningBlocker: It is easy to assume that once a verse establishes a principle for one case, it automatically applies elsewhere. Abba Shaul's reading shows that a single restrictive word in the verse can block exactly that kind of extension, leaving the morning order to follow the plain text instead.

takeaway.text: Whether the afternoon lamp-incense verse generalizes to the morning service remains disputed: the Rabbanan read it as a transferable principle, while Abba Shaul's reading of 'oto' confines it to the afternoon.

learning.ahaMoment: A single word - 'oto' - decides whether the afternoon lamp/incense verse is a universal principle or a one-time specification.
learning.memoryAnchor: Rabbanan: incense rides alongside lamps (morning too). Abba Shaul: 'oto' - that particular lamp, afternoon only.

argumentFlow.label: Rabbanan: afternoon analogy proves ketoret first
argumentFlow.speaker: Rabbanan
argumentFlow.text: The afternoon verse reads: 'when Aaron lights the lamps he shall burn incense.' So too in the morning: incense accompanies the lamp service. This proves our ruling that ketoret precedes the remaining lamps.

argumentFlow.label: Counter: does afternoon verse not imply lamps first?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: But the afternoon verse seems to say Aaron FIRST lights lamps THEN burns incense - would the Rabbanan accept this sequencing for the afternoon too?

argumentFlow.label: The verse means 'at the time of' - not after
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: 'At the time of lighting' means incense accompanies the lamp service, not that it comes after. The verse 'from evening to morning' teaches lamps burn all night - so incense is with the lighting, not following it.

argumentFlow.label: Abba Shaul: 'oto' limits the analogy
argumentFlow.speaker: Abba Shaul
argumentFlow.text: 'Oto' - that one lamp - restricts the afternoon verse to the afternoon situation. The analogy cannot extend to the morning service. The morning order follows the plain text.

misconceptions.misconception: 'At the time of lighting' means after the lighting is finished.
misconceptions.correction: Rashi clarifies it means during, accompanying the lamp service, not sequentially after it.

visualizableElements.item: Split diagram: Rabbanan (ketoret left, 5 lamps right, both morning) vs Abba Shaul (oto restricts afternoon only)
Exodus 30:8 with 'oto' highlighted and two interpretive arrows showing the Rabbanan and Abba Shaul readings

quizSeeds.question: How do the Rabbanan use the afternoon lamp verse to prove ketoret comes first?
quizSeeds.answer: They read 'at the time of lighting he shall burn incense' as meaning incense accompanies the lamps - so ketoret goes with (before) the remaining five lamps, not after.

quizSeeds.question: Why does Abba Shaul reject the Rabbanan's analogy?
quizSeeds.answer: The afternoon verse uses 'oto' (that one lamp), which limits the rule to that specific case and blocks its extension to the morning.

sugyot.finalRuling: Disputed: Rabbanan hold ketoret precedes lamps (morning analogy from afternoon); Abba Shaul holds 'oto' limits that analogy.

display.title: Can one mishna hold two views? Rav Pappa and Abaye disagree on method
display.oneLine: Rav Pappa resolves Yoma's internal contradiction by splitting it between two Tannaim; Abaye rejects that a single mishna can mix positions and recontextualizes the text instead.
display.whats: Rav Pappa and Abaye offer competing resolutions to the apparent contradiction in the mishnayot about the service order. Their disagreement hinges on whether a single mishna can incorporate two different tannaitic positions within one text. Rav Pappa says yes (different sections of Yoma reflect different Tannaim); Abaye says no (a mishna does not split its view).
display.hint: The machloket between Rav Pappa and Abaye is a methodological one: can a single tractate's mishnayot hold both R. Akiva and Abba Shaul's positions, or must each mishna be internally consistent?

learning.learnerQuestion: Two mishnayot in Yoma describe the service order differently. Can the same tractate simply follow different Tannaim in different chapters, or must each mishna speak with one voice?
learning.coreTension: Rav Pappa is willing to assign the two contradictory chapters to two different Tannaim, but Abaye holds a single mishna cannot mix tannaitic positions, so the same contradiction needs a different kind of resolution.
learning.coreMove: When Rav Pappa's chapter-splitting solution is itself shown to fail (Chapter 3 contradicts itself too), Abaye instead resolves the tension by reading one of the problematic passages as a general teaching about KG practice rather than a specific Yom Kippur sequence, avoiding the need to attribute different sections to different Tannaim at all.
learning.learningBlocker: It is tempting to treat this as a factual dispute about service order. The real disagreement is methodological: whether an anonymous mishna's internal sections can reflect different authorities, which is what determines whether chapter-splitting is even a legitimate solution.

takeaway.text: Resolving an apparent contradiction between mishnayot can require a methodological choice, not just a factual one: whether a single mishna may combine different tannaitic positions, or whether the text must instead be reread so no such split is needed.

learning.ahaMoment: Rav Pappa and Abaye are not disputing the facts but the methodology of Mishnah interpretation: can a tractate's sections reflect different anonymous authorities?
learning.memoryAnchor: Rav Pappa: the two chapters can follow different Tannaim. Abaye: a mishna cannot switch positions mid-text.

argumentFlow.label: Rav Pappa: different chapters, different Tannaim
argumentFlow.speaker: Rav Pappa
argumentFlow.text: Chapter 1 (two lamps) follows Rabbanan; Chapter 3 (five lamps) follows Abba Shaul. Different sections of Yoma can reflect different tannaitic views.

argumentFlow.label: But look at Chapter 3 - it contradicts itself too
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Chapter 3 says the KG offers the tamid last - but that contradicts Abba Shaul who has a different order. So assigning Chapter 3 to Abba Shaul doesn't work either.

argumentFlow.label: Abaye: a mishna cannot mix tannaitic positions
argumentFlow.speaker: Abaye
argumentFlow.text: The opening of the mishna (two lamps) follows Rabbanan and the later lotteries section (ketoret last) follows Abba Shaul - but a single mishna cannot split its ruling across different Tannaim. Abaye proposes an alternative reading.

argumentFlow.label: Abaye: the lotteries mishna is about a different context
argumentFlow.speaker: Abaye
argumentFlow.text: The Chapter 1 passage about 'all seven days he sprinkles' is not about Yom Kippur specifically but is teaching that the KG must be practiced in Temple service throughout the week - a general teaching, not a Yom Kippur sequence.

misconceptions.misconception: Rav Pappa and Abaye are disputing the actual halachic service order.
misconceptions.correction: They are disputing how to read the Mishnah's structure: whether a single mishna can hold two tannaitic positions, not what the correct order is.

visualizableElements.item: Two-column diagram: Rav Pappa's approach (Chapter 1 = Rabbanan, Chapter 3 = Abba Shaul) vs Abaye's approach (mishna cannot split positions)
Mishna chapter 1 vs chapter 3 content shown side by side with the contradiction highlighted

quizSeeds.question: How do Rav Pappa and Abaye each resolve the contradiction between the two Yoma mishnayot?
quizSeeds.answer: Rav Pappa assigns the two chapters to different Tannaim. Abaye objects that a mishna cannot split its position and instead recontextualizes the problematic passage.

quizSeeds.question: What is the methodological principle Abaye uses to reject Rav Pappa's solution?
quizSeeds.answer: A single mishna cannot represent two different tannaitic positions within itself - it must be internally consistent.

sugyot.finalRuling: No definitive ruling given; the sugya presents both positions as live options.
prerequisiteKnowledge: Abba Shaul vs Rabbanan positions on ketoret order

display.title: Tamid as olah and chatat at once: the hekesh forces an unprecedented combination
display.oneLine: R. Shimon ish HaMitzpah's corner-based scheme satisfies the tamid's dual olah-and-chatat requirement because Scripture's hekesh forces the combination; a cleaner height-based alternative is tested afterward and fails for lack of precedent.
display.whats: The Gemara investigates the basis for R. Shimon ish HaMitzpah's ruling that changes the tamid's blood application. The ordinary practice gives the tamid's blood two separate diagonal corner-applications: first a sprinkling at the northeast corner, then, as a separate later step, a sprinkling at the southwest corner. R. Shimon ish HaMitzpah leaves the northeast application unchanged but splits only the southwest application into two separate single-wall sprinklings (west, then south) instead of one diagonal throw. The Gemara ties this to R. Yochanan's teaching that the tamid, though an olah, must also be performed with the procedure of a chatat; a fuller combination (complete four-horn chatat plus complete two-corner olah) is tested and refuted because blood cannot be made to atone a second time, so Scripture's own hekesh is taken to force R. Shimon's otherwise unprecedented corner-based combination instead. A further height-based alternative (below=olah, above=chatat) is then tested and rejected for lack of precedent, confirming R. Shimon's corner-based scheme as the one that stands.
display.hint: The tamid is an unusual sacrifice. R. Shimon says it must be treated as BOTH an olah (two-corner sprinkling) AND a chatat (four-horn-style application). A full combination of both fails since blood can't atone twice - so Scripture's own hekesh is what forces R. Shimon's corner-based scheme through instead. A later height-based alternative is tried and also fails for lack of precedent.

learning.learnerQuestion: If the tamid is fundamentally an olah, what is the textual basis for also requiring a chatat-style application, and does R. Shimon ish HaMitzpah's already-known corner-splitting ruling actually satisfy that requirement - or would a cleaner combination work better?
learning.coreTension: R. Yochanan teaches that a verse (juxtaposing the Yom Kippur goat-chatat with the daily tamid-olah) forces the Merciful One's own hekesh: the tamid, though an olah, must also receive a chatat-style act. R. Shimon's existing ruling - one throw at the northeast corner standing in for the olah component, two throws at the southwest standing in for the chatat component - satisfies this only because Scripture itself forces an otherwise unprecedented combination; a fuller combination (a complete four-horn chatat application plus a complete two-corner olah application) is rejected outright, since we have no precedent for blood atoning twice or for blood that is half chatat and half olah.
learning.coreMove: After the hekesh resolves the basic difficulty (an unprecedented combination is acceptable because Scripture forces it), the Gemara tests whether a more elegant, precedented alternative exists: splitting the chatat/olah distinction by height (below vs. above) instead of by corner. It is rejected for lack of precedent, and two candidate precedents from the Yom Kippur inner-sanctum blood service are each raised and explained away as not being true height-splits, leaving R. Shimon's corner-based scheme as the one actually implemented.
learning.learningBlocker: It is tempting to think the Gemara is searching for any workable combination and ends in failure. In fact the combination already exists and is already implemented (R. Shimon's ruling from step-01); what the Gemara does afterward is test whether a different, more precedented method could have achieved the same result, and shows that it could not - which reinforces, rather than undermines, the hekesh-based resolution.

takeaway.text: R. Shimon ish HaMitzpah's corner-based split (northeast unchanged, southwest divided into west-then-south) stands as the implementation of the tamid's dual olah-and-chatat requirement, because Scripture's own hekesh forces an otherwise unprecedented combination. A height-based alternative (below=olah, above=chatat) is considered and rejected for lack of precedent, even after two Yom Kippur inner-altar blood-sprinklings are raised as possible precedents and explained away.

learning.ahaMoment: The Gemara doesn't reject R. Shimon's ruling - it defends it. After the hekesh justifies the existing corner-based scheme as scripturally forced, the Gemara looks for a tidier, precedented alternative (splitting by height instead of by corner), fails to find one even after testing two candidate precedents from the Yom Kippur service, and so confirms that the corner-based scheme is the one that stands.
learning.memoryAnchor: Tamid = olah forced by hekesh to also get a chatat-act. R. Shimon's corner-split already satisfies this. A height-based alternative is tried and fails for lack of precedent - the original ruling wins by default.

argumentFlow.label: Ordinary practice vs. R. Shimon's change: splitting the southwest application
argumentFlow.speaker: R. Shimon ish HaMitzpah
argumentFlow.text: The ordinary practice: the priest comes to the northeast corner and sprinkles once there, then proceeds to the southwest corner and sprinkles once there - two separate diagonal corner-applications. R. Shimon ish HaMitzpah changes only the daily offering's southwest application: the northeast corner is sprinkled as usual, but at the southwest corner he instead sprinkles once on the west side and then separately on the south side, rather than one diagonal throw covering both.

argumentFlow.label: R. Yochanan's hekesh: the tamid's olah blood must also carry a chatat-act
argumentFlow.speaker: R. Yochanan (in the name of the house of R. Yannai)
argumentFlow.text: The verse juxtaposes the Yom Kippur goat-chatat with the daily tamid-olah, and the Merciful One says: perform a chatat-act with it. How so? Give one throw that counts as two, in the manner of olah (the northeast corner), and two throws that count as two, in the manner of chatat (the southwest corner, split west-then-south) - this is exactly R. Shimon ish HaMitzpah's already-stated ruling from step-01.

argumentFlow.label: A fuller combination is proposed and refuted
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Why not instead give a complete doubled olah application (two-that-are-four) and a complete separate chatat application (four-that-are-four)? Rejected: we have no precedent for blood that atones and then atones again, and we have no precedent for blood that is half chatat and half olah.

argumentFlow.label: The hekesh forces the combination despite the lack of precedent
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rather, perforce, Scripture juxtaposed them - the combination is unprecedented but scripturally forced, so R. Shimon's corner-based scheme stands. The Gemara notes a parallel: elsewhere too Scripture forces an unprecedented juxtaposition by hekesh, but there it amounts to a mere division of the gifts, not a true dual-identity problem.

argumentFlow.label: Alternative proposal: split by height instead of by corner - refuted
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Why not instead give one throw below, in the manner of olah, and two throws above, in the manner of chatat? Rejected: we have no precedent for blood that is half above and half below.

argumentFlow.label: Two Yom Kippur precedents are tested and explained away; R. Shimon's scheme stands
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Two candidate precedents for a height-based blood split are raised from the Yom Kippur inner-sanctum service - the bull's blood sprinkled one-above-seven-below 'like one who flogs' on the curtain, and the blood sprinkled seven times on the altar's 'pure part' - and each is explained away as not a true locational height-split (the flogging motion is continuous, not a fixed half-split; the 'pure part' refers to the object itself, not half its height). No precedent for a height-based split survives, so R. Shimon's corner-based scheme from step-01 remains the implementation that stands.

sourceRefs.note: Yom Kippur precedents tested and explained away

misconceptions.misconception: R. Shimon ish HaMitzpah's ruling is itself the proposal being tested and rejected by the Gemara.
misconceptions.correction: R. Shimon's corner-based scheme (step-01) is the ruling already in effect; R. Yochanan's hekesh (step-02) justifies it. The Gemara's subsequent proposals and refutations (steps 03-06) test whether a different, more precedented scheme could replace it - and conclude it could not.

misconceptions.misconception: The sugya ends in an unresolved teiku, leaving R. Shimon's ruling without a workable implementation.
misconceptions.correction: The sugya is resolved at step-04: Scripture's own hekesh forces the otherwise unprecedented corner-based combination. The later height-based alternative (steps 05-06) is a secondary exploration that fails for lack of precedent, which reinforces rather than undermines the resolution.

visualizableElements.item: Two-step diagram of the ordinary practice (diagonal sprinkling at northeast, then a separate diagonal sprinkling at southwest) alongside R. Shimon ish HaMitzpah's change, which leaves northeast untouched and splits only the southwest sprinkling into two single-wall throws (west, then south)

quizSeeds.question: Why does R. Shimon ish HaMitzpah's corner-based scheme for the tamid's blood count as valid, despite having no prior precedent?
quizSeeds.answer: Because Scripture's own hekesh (juxtaposing the Yom Kippur goat-chatat with the daily tamid-olah) forces the combination - an unprecedented blood-application scheme is acceptable when the verse itself demands it.

quizSeeds.question: What alternative to R. Shimon's corner-based split does the Gemara test afterward, and why does it fail?
quizSeeds.answer: A height-based split (below=olah, above=chatat). It fails for lack of precedent - even after two Yom Kippur inner-altar blood-sprinklings are raised as possible precedents, each is explained away as not a true height-split.

sugyot.finalRuling: Resolved: R. Shimon ish HaMitzpah's corner-based scheme (northeast unchanged, southwest split west-then-south) stands as the tamid's dual olah-and-chatat implementation, because Scripture's hekesh forces an otherwise unprecedented combination. A height-based alternative is tested and rejected for lack of precedent, confirming the corner-based scheme as the one actually practiced.

rashiTranslations.en: 'From evening until morning' - regarding the lamps it is written, 'Aaron and his sons shall set it in order from evening until
morning.' 'Give it' - to the candelabrum a measure of oil so that it burns the whole night; and the Sages estimated
The Sages: half a log for each lamp, enough to keep it burning the whole night of the season of
Tevet; and if oil is left over on a shorter night, let it remain. 'You have no service that is valid' - meaning there is no
daytime service that remains valid after their lighting,
for he expounds it this way: 'it' must be tended from evening until morning,
and not anything else, from evening until morning. 'For it is written'
'it' - as I explained, and it must be that at the time of
the lighting there must be a burning of incense, is what is meant;
but in the morning, by the order implied in the verse's own meaning,
the order of service is that he tends it and only then burns it
'Rav Pappa said, it is not difficult' - the order
of the day against the order of the day, etc.: regarding the cleaning of two
lamps, that which we learned puts the incense first is the Rabbis' view,
and that which we learned puts the lamps first is Abba Shaul's view
'To the mishna here' - that of the first chapter (14a)
'The lottery' - that of the mishna of the lotteries taught in the
second chapter (25a), which teaches that the incense comes last,
following Abba Shaul. 'Say the latter clause' - of the order-of-the-day
passage, taught in the third chapter (31b): 'They brought
him the daily offering, to the High Priest, on the day
of Atonement.' 'He cut it' - he cut it with a cut in it
that renders the slaughter valid, through the majority of the two organs but not all of them,
since he himself needs to hurry and take
the bowl to receive the blood, for none of the day of Atonement's
service is valid except through him
'And to tend the lamps' - and this must
refer to the last two, since there is
no opinion that the incense precedes all five lamps
'The first and last clauses' - of the order-of-the-day passage are the Rabbis'
view, etc. - in astonishment, since this whole tractate is like one mishna
entirely occupied with the order, in that
the passages are arranged and proceed in sequence
'Does the tanna teach first, etc.' - in astonishment, that Abaye establishes
the mishna of the first chapter as the cleaning of two
lamps, and that of the second chapter as the cleaning of five lamps
'And Abaye says to you' - that which is taught in the first chapter,
that all seven days he tosses the blood, etc., does not
refer to Yom Kippur itself and is not particular
about the order; rather it speaks only of instruction in general,
teaching us that the High Priest must be
occupied with the service all seven days, so that he
becomes practiced and ready in it for Yom Kippur;
and the actual order of the day he teaches elsewhere; therefore he taught
the cleaning of five in the second chapter, and taught in the third chapter
the cleaning of two. 'As a sin-offering to the Lord, in addition to'
'the daily burnt-offering' - the act of a sin-offering is done upon
the daily burnt-offering; and since a sin-offering requires its blood-placements to be divided
among the corners, for its blood is placed on all four
corners, the daily burnt-offering too has its blood-placement
divided; not that its status as a burnt-offering is thereby annulled from
it, for it remains a burnt-offering, but rather
both procedures apply to it. 'Four that are four' -
on all four corners. 'We do not find blood'
that atones' - one atonement of its own,
and then goes on to atone a second, separate atonement
'It is merely a division of the blood-placements' - since
both placements are on a single corner, there is no proof here of
an actual sin-offering procedure. 'So then let him place one, etc.' -

the blood of a burnt-offering is placed below the scarlet thread, and the blood of a sin-offering above it; and since this latter placement, the one that divides the two, is done for the sake of the sin-offering procedure,

it ought to be placed above, like a sin-offering. 'He sprinkles from it, etc.' - later, in the fifth chapter (53b), when he sprinkles from the blood of the bull opposite the thickness of the Ark-cover, and it was assumed

that this means one sprinkling from the middle of its thickness upward, and seven from its middle downward. 'And he answers: like one who lashes' - this wording of 'downward and upward' that was taught does not refer to the exact middle point; rather, he places the first

sprinkling toward the top, and the seven beneath it, each one lower than the one before, like one who lashes. 'Like a lash-wielder' - like a court officer who strikes with the strap, each blow lower than the one before, since he does not strike in one

place; but the word 'matzlif' itself I do not know the source of. 'He sprinkled on the pure surface of the inner altar seven times' - as it is stated, 'and he shall sprinkle upon it from the blood,' etc. 'Against half of it' - opposite

the middle of the height of its wall. 'Tihara' - midday, half the day; and since the sprinkler performed seven sprinklings, it is impossible to be so precise that none of them fall either above or below the exact midpoint
'Against its own body' - the daf ends here; the comment (explaining that this refers to the altar's own roof) continues on 15b.
